title_en: Sermon to the People of the Church of Caesarea
author: Augustine of Hippo
addressee: The Catholic congregation of Caesarea in Mauretania
occasion: Augustine addresses the Catholic congregation at Caesarea after Emeritus, the Donatist bishop of the city, has been brought into the church and has begun a public conversation with him. The people have shouted 'here or nowhere,' and Augustine explains why he seeks Emeritus's reconciliation and urges the congregation to pray for his conversion.
argument: Augustine rejoices that Emeritus has said he cannot refuse what the Catholics want, namely peace and unity, and urges the people to pray that he will quickly abandon his present wish to remain in schism. He explains that Donatists are received as brothers because the baptism and faith they possess belong to Christ, not to Donatus, and that these gifts are useless without charity, which is found only in Catholic unity. He argues that Emeritus, like a lost sheep bearing the Lord's mark, must be sought precisely because he has the sign of peace without possessing peace itself. He answers the objection that the Donatists suffered persecution by showing from their own claims about Caecilian that even the unrighteous can be persecuted by those claiming to be righteous, and that the question is not whether one suffers but for what cause. He concludes by affirming the people's cry 'here or nowhere,' praying that Emeritus will be won to unity.

outline.move: Augustine reports Emeritus's opening words, explains that Emeritus cannot ultimately refuse what the Catholics want, and asks the congregation to pray for him after they shout 'here or nowhere.'

Augustine explains that Donatists are received not as heretics but as Catholics to be changed, because the baptism and invocation they have belong to Christ, not to Donatus, just as a deserter still bears the emperor's mark.
He argues from 1 Corinthians 13 that sacraments, prophecy, knowledge, and faith are great goods but profit nothing without charity.

He addresses Emeritus as a lost sheep bearing the Lord's sign, and describes baptism as a title of peace posted on a house where discord dwells, which must be driven out so that peace may possess what bears its title.

He challenges Emeritus to prove he has charity by holding unity, and uses the examples of Ishmael and the sons of Jacob's handmaids to show that birth outside the lawful wife does not exclude from the inheritance if pride is abandoned.
He declares that outside the Catholic Church one can have honor, sacraments, and even martyrdom, but not salvation, since even giving one's body to be burned profits nothing without charity.

He recalls the Donatists' own admission at Carthage that their forebears persecuted Caecilian, and argues that if the righteous can persecute the unrighteous, the question is not whether one suffers but for what cause.

He defends his own pursuit of Emeritus as a persecution of blasphemy against the church, and contrasts it with the violence once done by the Donatists at Constantina, where a certain Petilianus forcibly baptized and ordained a Catholic catechumen.
He affirms the people's cry 'here or nowhere,' prays that Emeritus will choose 'here' in peace and unity, and commits the outcome to God.

cast.name: Emeritus
cast.who: Donatist bishop of Caesarea, present in the church and in dialogue with Augustine.

cast.name: Deuterius
cast.who: Catholic bishop of Caesarea, Augustine's fellow bishop.

cast.name: Caecilian
cast.who: Catholic bishop of Carthage whom the first Donatists accused and persecuted.

cast.name: Donatus
cast.who: Founder of the Donatist schism; Augustine insists he did not baptize in his own name.

cast.name: Petilianus
cast.who: The Donatist who forcibly baptized and ordained a Catholic catechumen; he was the perpetrator of violence, not the victim. The victim is unnamed.

cast.name: Ishmael
cast.who: Son of Abraham by Hagar, disinherited for pride.

cast.name: Isaac
cast.who: Son of Abraham and Sarah, heir of the promise.

cast.name: Sarah
cast.who: Abraham's wife, who arranged for Abraham to have a son through her maidservant Hagar, and later had Ishmael disinherited for pride.

cast.name: Rachel
cast.who: Jacob's wife, named as a type of the church whose baptism is shared.

cast.name: Jacob
cast.who: Patriarch whose sons by handmaids shared one inheritance.

voices.speaker: Emeritus
voices.how_marked: Augustine quotes his opening words directly and later addresses him in the second person, sometimes voicing his objections.

voices.speaker: The congregation
voices.how_marked: Their acclamation is reported: 'aut hic aut nusquam.'

voices.speaker: Paul the Apostle
voices.how_marked: Quoted from his epistles, introduced by 'ait apostolus' or similar formulas.

voices.speaker: The Donatists
voices.how_marked: Their claims are quoted or paraphrased, introduced by 'dicunt,' 'dixerunt,' or 'contenderunt.'

voices.speaker: The Psalmist
voices.how_marked: Quoted from the Psalms, introduced by 'dicit psalmus' or 'in psalmo.'

voices.speaker: The Lord (in the Gospel and Revelation)
voices.how_marked: Quoted as words of Christ or of the seer in Revelation.

key_terms.sense: The unity of the Catholic Church, which Emeritus is urged to enter.
The Donatist separation from the Catholic Church.
Those separated from the Catholic Church, as the Donatists are, though they are received as Catholics when they change.
The mark or seal of baptism and ordination, which belongs to Christ the emperor, not to the deserter Donatus.
One who has left the Catholic Church, especially the first schismatics; later Donatists are signed by deserters but bear the emperor's mark.
The love without which all sacraments and even martyrdom profit nothing; identified with holding Catholic unity.
The peace Christ gives, identified with the unity and inheritance of the Catholic Church.
Baptism as a sign or inscription of peace posted on a person in whom discord dwells.
The Donatist party or communion, as opposed to the Catholic Church.
The universal Catholic Church, outside which there is no salvation.
Pursuit or harassment, which Augustine argues can be righteous when directed against blasphemy and for the sake of unity.
The inheritance of peace and the promise, shared by all who hold unity, regardless of where they were baptized.
Suffering or death for a cause, which profits nothing without charity and outside the Catholic Church.

scripture: Augustine quotes from the Old Latin version of the Psalms with Septuagint numbering, and from the Gospels and Pauline epistles in Old Latin forms. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and, for the Psalms, the Hebrew numbering with a note where the Septuagint numbering differs.
uncertain: The exact date of the sermon; 418 is the commonly accepted date based on the context of Augustine's visit to Caesarea in Mauretania, but the source does not state it.
The precise identity of 'Petialius' and the spelling of his name; the source form is uncertain and may be a textual corruption.
Whether Emeritus was physically present throughout the sermon or had left before its conclusion.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Augustine addresses the Catholic congregation at Caesarea after Emeritus, the Donatist bishop of the city, has been brought into the church and has begun a public conversation with him.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: mox ut ingressus est istam ecclesiam, illo loco stans ubi primum coepimus cum eo colloquium
_unresolved_facts.fix: Augustine addresses the Catholic congregation at Caesarea while Emeritus, the Donatist bishop of the city, is present in the church and has begun a public conversation with him. The sermon occurs during this encounter, not after it has concluded.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He answers the objection that the Donatists suffered persecution by showing from their own claims about Caecilian that even the unrighteous can be persecuted by those claiming to be righteous, and that the question is not whether one suffers but for what cause.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: si iniqui erant, desere iniquos, ueni ad nos; si autem sancti erant, potest ergo fieri ut sancti persequantur iniustum. noli nobis irasci, si persequimur, noli dicere: iniusti estis qui persequimini. iam enim ostendistis, quia fieri potest ut et iusti persequantur iniustum.
_unresolved_facts.fix: He answers the objection that the Donatists suffered persecution by showing from their own claims about Caecilian that even the righteous can persecute the unrighteous, and that the question is not whether one suffers but for what cause. Augustine argues that if the Donatists' forebears were righteous in persecuting Caecilian (as they claimed), then righteous people can indeed persecute the unrighteous; if they were unrighteous, the Donatists should abandon them.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He declares that outside the Catholic Church one can have honor, sacraments, and even martyrdom, but not salvation, since even giving one's body to be burned profits nothing without charity.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: si tradidero corpus meum ut ardeam, caritatem autem non habeam, nihil mihi prodest. ego non dico: si aliquas iniurias quasi iactet se passum esse pro parte Donati aut aliqua damna terrena, nihil ei prodest. ego plus dico: si patiatur foris inimicum Christi, non catholicum fratrem suum quaerentem salutem eius, sed inimicum Christi si foras patiatur et dicat ei foras ab ecclesia Christi inimicus Christi: 'pone thus idolis, adora deos meos', et non adorans occidatur ab inimico Christi, sanguinem fundere potest, coronam accipere non potest.
_unresolved_facts.fix: He declares that outside the Catholic Church one can have honor, sacraments, and even give one's blood to be shed (sanguinem fundere), but not salvation or the martyr's crown, since even giving one's body to be burned profits nothing without charity. Augustine explicitly denies that dying outside the church counts as martyrdom: 'sanguinem fundere potest, coronam accipere non potest' (he can shed blood, but cannot receive the crown).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Petilianus: The Donatist who forcibly baptized and ordained a Catholic catechumen; he was the perpetrator of violence, not the victim. The victim is unnamed.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Petialius tenuit, uim fecit nolenti, scrutatus est fugientem, inuenit latentem, extraxit pauentem, baptizauit trementem, ordinauit nolentem
_unresolved_facts.fix: Petilianus: A Donatist at Constantina who forcibly baptized and ordained a Catholic catechumen. The victim is unnamed. Note: The source form is 'Petialius,' not 'Petilianus'; this may be a textual variant or corruption.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Lord (in the Gospel and Revelation): Quoted as words of Christ or of the seer in Revelation. sections: [1, 5]
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Lord (in the Gospel and Revelation): Quoted as words of Christ or of the seer in Revelation. sections: [1, 4, 5] — In section 4, Augustine addresses Christ directly: 'o Christe, qui es pax nostra, qui fecisti utraque unum. fac nos unum...' and again 'tu muta istum contradictorem, qui una hora in cruce mutasti latronem.'

Paul the Apostle: sections: [1, 2, 3, 5] — In section 5, Augustine quotes/paraphrases Paul: 'numquid Paulus pro uobis crucifixus est? quid uultis esse mei et non magis domini mei? quid uultis esse mei et non potius cuius ego sum? agnoscite, aduertite characterem uestrum: numquid in nomine Pauli baptizati estis?'
The Psalmist: sections: [3, 4, 5, 8] — In section 5, Augustine quotes Psalm 132[133]: 'ecce quam bonum et quam iucundum habitare fratres in unum.'
Petialius: Petilianus (with note that the source form 'Petialius' is uncertain and may be a textual corruption; the standard form of the name is Petilianus)
